# Separate condenser (Watt) (`separate_condenser`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: needs atmospheric_engine; helped by boring_machine, heat_energy_conservation, air_pump_vacuum, thermometer_temperature
- Core idea: Newcomen's engine wastes most of its steam reheating a cylinder that the injection water has just chilled. Keep the cylinder always hot and condense the steam elsewhere: connect the cylinder by a pipe and valve to a separate vessel kept cold in a tank of water. When the valve opens the steam rushes into that vessel and condenses there. Watt's full-size pumping engine also used an air pump to draw the condensate and leaked air out of the condenser, a steam jacket and lagging round the cylinder, and a closed cylinder top with a stuffing box for the piston rod, so that steam instead of cold air presses the piston down. On the return stroke an equalising valve connects the two sides of the piston, allowing the pump rods to draw it back up. Fuel use could fall by about three quarters. Because a water seal can no longer lie on the piston, the cylinder must be bored truly round.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying Watt invented the steam engine, or was inspired by a kettle; he improved Newcomen's engine after repairing a model of one
  - A condenser without an air pump fills with air and warm water and stops working
  - Confusing a working model with a full-size cylinder: Watt demonstrated separate condensation in 1765, but leakage around large pistons wasted steam until machining improved
  - Assuming it makes the engine stronger; it makes it cheaper to run
- History: europe: 1763–1764 – Watt repairs Glasgow University's model Newcomen engine; 1765 idea of the separate condenser; 1769 patent; 1776 first engines at work (Bloomfield colliery and Wilkinson's ironworks) in partnership with Matthew Boulton; patent extended to 1800
- Read:
  - H. W. Dickinson & Rhys Jenkins, James Watt and the Steam Engine (1927)
  - Richard L. Hills, Power from Steam: A History of the Stationary Steam Engine (1989)
  - Ben Marsden, Watt's Perfect Engine: Steam and the Age of Invention (2002)
